Nehiloth
NEH-hih-loth
noun
Hebrew nechīlōth, of uncertain root; by the most received account from chālīl, “a pipe, a flute” (the bored or perforated reed), thus wind instruments; it has of old been understood of the flutes or wind instruments.

Biblical Definition

Nehiloth appears but once in all the Scriptures, in the title of the fifth psalm: “To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David” (Psa 5, title). The word is obscure, yet most have understood it of wind instruments — the pipe or flute, the breath-driven reed — as the King James translators noted in their margin. The psalm it heads is David’s morning prayer: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psa 5:3). If Nehiloth indeed names the flute, then the whole instrument of man is here brought to the worship of God — the strings of Neginoth and the breath of Nehiloth alike, that nothing in the worshipper be withheld. The psalmist bids the saints praise the LORD “with stringed instruments and organs” (Psa 150:4), the breath of life returned in song to Him who gave it. Let the believer take warning too from the very obscurity of the term: there are things in the inspired text we cannot now fully expound, and humility, not invention, becomes us there. What is plain is enough — that David rose early to seek his God, and would have his every faculty, breath and voice and instrument, consecrated to that holy end.

Webster 1828 Definition

Wind instruments, or flutes; the obscure direction over David’s morning prayer in the fifth psalm.

NEHILOTH, a Hebrew word found only in the title of the fifth psalm.

It is most received as denoting wind instruments, the pipe or flute, and it is of old understood of the flutes or wind instruments.

It heads David’s morning prayer, in which he directs his prayer unto the LORD and looks up.

If it names the flute, it brings the breath of man, with the strings, into the worship of God.

Its very obscurity teaches humility before what the inspired text does not fully unfold.

Key Scripture

Psa 5, title — "To the chief Musician upon Nehiloth, A Psalm of David."

Psa 5:3 — "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up."

Psa 150:4 — "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs."

Psa 5:7 — "But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple."

Modern Corruption

An obscure worship-direction, not a contested doctrine; it teaches humility before what the inspired text does not unfold, and the consecration of every faculty to God.

expand to see more

Nehiloth faces no postmodern redefinition. The lesson of its obscurity cuts rather against a perennial fault of the proud heart — the refusal to let any word stand unmastered, the itch to invent a certainty where the LORD has left a holy reticence. The word means, most likely, the flute; beyond that the godly are content not to press.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: humility before the text, and the consecration of the whole man to worship. David rose in the morning and looked up; he would have voice and breath and instrument alike laid upon the altar of praise. The saint gives God not a part but the whole — every faculty, every early hour, every breath that He first gave.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew most likely meaning flutes, Nehiloth heads David’s morning prayer and teaches the consecration of every faculty to God.
